name: PhotonLibOS io_uring vs epoll echo-server comparison
workload: Coroutine-based echo server (ping-pong and streaming/multiplexed client modes), single-connection QPS/throughput at buffer sizes 64B-16KB, PhotonLibOS's io_uring backend vs its epoll backend, on 2 cloud VMs
claimed_speedup: Streaming mode, buf=64B: epoll 1,565K qps / 780Mb/s vs io_uring 506K qps / 260Mb/s (epoll ~3.1x faster); buf=16384B: epoll 224K qps / 27.3Gb/s vs io_uring 183K qps / 22.5Gb/s (epoll ~1.2x faster). Author separately states io_uring 'can always surpass' epoll in ping-pong-mode workloads, but gives no numbers for that case in this thread
hardware: 2x Intel Xeon Platinum 8369B @2.70GHz cloud VMs, 96 cores/128GB RAM, 40Gb network, CentOS 8, kernel 6.0.7
tradeoffs: Result is workload-shape-dependent: io_uring wins ping-pong (single round-trip) workloads but loses to epoll in streaming/multiplexed (IO-depth=1) workloads in this test; the gap narrows as buffer size grows; author also found plain psync 3-4x faster than io_uring for pure in-memory (tmpfs) IO at IO depth 1
caveats: This is a negative/mixed result for io_uring vs epoll in streaming mode specifically -- included as evidence for the already-catalogued PhotonLibOS entry, not as a new 'faster than epoll' candidate; no compiler/build flags stated; the ping-pong-mode numbers (where io_uring reportedly wins) are not shown in this thread

hardware: Haswell Intel Core i5-4278U, turbo disabled

name: LSQUIC
workload: "QUIC on the Highway" (Koenig, Zirngibl et al., ACM IMC 2023): an adaptation of the QUIC Interop Runner run on dedicated (non-virtualized) 10G-linked physical hosts, measuring HTTP/3 goodput for six QUIC implementations (aioquic, quic-go, mvfst, picoquic, quiche, LSQUIC) across buffer-size configurations.
claimed_speedup: ~1.28x quiche with buffer tuning (derived from page data): verbatim, "LSQUIC reaches a goodput of 3250 Mbit/s, an 8.7% increase compared to the baseline" (largest tested buffer) vs quiche buffer tuning that "increase[s] the goodput but only by 3% to 2530 Mbit/s"; the paper separately states goodput across all six implementations and buffer settings ranges "52 Mbit/s to 3004 Mbit/s", and names LSQUIC and quiche as "the two best-performing implementations" of the six tested
hardware: AMD EPYC 7543 (32-core), 512GB RAM, Broadcom BCM57416 NICs as primary configuration; additional runs on AMD EPYC 7551P and several Intel Xeon models
tradeoffs: The margin over quiche here is narrow (~1.28x) and buffer-tuning-dependent, not a decisive win; the paper frames LSQUIC and quiche as roughly co-best of the six implementations it tested, not LSQUIC as a clear outright leader.
caveats: LSQUIC is already catalogued on KNOWN_LIST; included here only as new Tier B evidence of it beating the in-scope baseline quiche, per the orchestrator's is_evidence_for_known exception (GitHub hosts the paper's companion benchmark/analysis code at https://github.com/tumi8/quic-10g-paper, which is public but has no declared license and was not independently checked for exact compiler/flag settings used per-implementation, capping this at Tier B rather than A despite public code and stated CPU hardware).
found_via: arXiv: export.arxiv.org query "QUIC performance comparison" -> arXiv 2309.16395 "QUIC on the Highway: Evaluating Performance on High-rate Links"; companion code at github.com/tumi8/quic-10g-paper

name: LSQUIC
workload: 8 GB file download over HTTP/3 on a dedicated 10 Gbit/s link between AMD EPYC 7543 servers, all client/server implementation pairs, 50 repeated runs, measuring goodput (bytes transferred / time)
claimed_speedup: Matched client/server pairs, default config: LSQUIC-LSQUIC 3004 Mbit/s vs quiche-quiche baseline 2506 Mbit/s (~1.2x). With increased UDP receive buffers and arch-tuned compile flags (LSQUIC*/quiche*): LSQUIC-LSQUIC 3882 Mbit/s vs quiche-quiche 2590 Mbit/s (~1.5x). On the newest test CPU (Intel Xeon Gold 6312U), optimized LSQUIC approaches ~5 Gbit/s.
compiler_and_flags: Debian Bullseye, Linux 5.10.0-8-amd64; LSQUIC* variant built with architecture-specific compile flags (exact flags in the paper's companion repo, not fully enumerated in the PDF text)
hardware: AMD EPYC 7543 32-core (primary); also AMD EPYC 7551P, Intel Xeon D-1518, Intel Xeon E5-1650, Intel Xeon Gold 6312U (cross-CPU comparison in Fig. 9)
tradeoffs: C API (less ergonomic than Rust quiche); goodput is highly sensitive to UDP buffer sizing, CPU generation, and cipher (LSQUIC drops to 30-70% of Cubic goodput when misconfigured with BBR); cross-implementation pairing is asymmetric -- quiche-server+LSQUIC-client reaches 2556 Mbit/s but LSQUIC-server+quiche-client only 1186 Mbit/s, more than 2x lower, so the win is config/direction dependent, not a uniform speedup
caveats: Paper's baseline measurements are from ~January 2023 software versions of both libraries; QUIC implementations change quickly so current relative standing may differ. quiche itself is one of the four named category baselines, so this is evidence for a KNOWN_LIST project (LSQUIC) beating a baseline, not a new discovery.
found_via: arXiv search 'QUIC implementations performance comparison goodput' -> 'QUIC on the Highway: Evaluating Performance on High-rate Links' (Jaeger, Zirngibl, Kempf, Ploch, Carle; IFIP Networking 2023), code at github.com/tumi8/quic-10g-paper

name: Unbound
workload: DNS Shotgun load test measuring maximum sustained queries answered per second over a 120s window, per transport (UDP, DoT, DoH-GET, DoH-POST), against a fixed real-world query trace, for Knot Resolver 6.2.0/5.7.6, Unbound 1.24.2, and BIND 9.20.18/9.21.17

Unbound is already on KNOWN_LIST; reported here only as is_evidence_for_known against BIND9, a widely used incumbent not on the baseline list.

name: cmd-stream (TCP + MUS codec) -- third-party benchmark vs gRPC/Protobuf
workload: Echo requests over TCP: 1/2/4/8/16 concurrent Go clients, each firing all requests simultaneously in separate goroutines, payload sizes 17-1024 bytes, fixed 30ms server-side response delay; QPS benchmark run via `go test -bench BenchmarkQPS`
claimed_speedup: cmd-stream (TCP, MUS codec) 145352 QPS at 1 client vs grpc_http2_protobuf 46142 QPS (~3.15x), and 288727 QPS at 16 clients vs grpc_http2_protobuf 63285 QPS (~4.56x) (derived from page data, results/qps/qps.csv)
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.24.1, default `go test -bench` build (no explicit -gcflags / optimization flags stated beyond the Go toolchain version)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U with Radeon Graphics, Debian 6.1.148-1 x86_64 GNU/Linux (laptop, charger connected, fan at full speed)
tradeoffs: Independent third-party benchmark repo (by ymz-ncnk, likely the mus-format/cmd-stream author) rather than a peer-reviewed or vendor-neutral suite; also exercises cmd-stream's own MUS serialization format (also KNOWN_LIST) rather than isolating transport from codec.
caveats: cmd-stream/cmd-stream-go and mus-format/mus-go are both already on KNOWN_LIST; reported here only as new Tier A evidence of cmd-stream (using MUS) beating the in-scope baseline gRPC, per the orchestrator's is_evidence_for_known exception. Benchmark is single-laptop, single-run-family (10 iterations via -count=10) rather than datacenter-scale; DRPC (a different framework in the same suite) is separately noted to hit a head-of-line-blocking ceiling, but that does not apply to the cmd-stream vs gRPC numbers cited here.

name: AWS-LC
workload: Full TLS handshake connections/sec (server-only) and TLS session-resumption connections/sec under HAProxy, on a 64-core AWS Graviton4 instance, across OpenSSL 1.1.1/3.0.x/3.1-3.4-dev, AWS-LC, and WolfSSL.
claimed_speedup: Full handshake: AWS-LC (optimized, RSA opts + CMAKE_C_STANDARD=11) 63,000+ conn/sec vs OpenSSL 1.1.1 ~48,000 and OpenSSL 3.0.2 ~21,000 (up to ~3x vs OpenSSL 3.0.2). TLS resumption (with HAProxy low-overhead locks): AWS-LC (C11 build) 183,000 conn/sec vs OpenSSL 1.1.1 124,000, OpenSSL 3.0.14 8,000 (AWS-LC ~23x), and OpenSSL 3.0.2 1,500-1,600 (AWS-LC ~114-122x, collapsing above 16 threads due to lock contention).
compiler_and_flags: gcc-11.4; AWS-LC rebuilt with CMAKE_C_STANDARD=11 (vs default C99) to enable atomics instead of pthread locks; HAProxy built with USE_PTHREAD_EMULATION=1 for low-overhead locks
hardware: AWS r8g.16xlarge, 64 Graviton4 (ARM Neoverse V2) cores, Ubuntu 22.04
license: Apache-2.0 (ISC and OpenSSL license portions for imported code)
stars_or_usage: used in production AWS services (s2n-tls, AWS SDKs); GitHub page showed ~835 stars at fetch time
tradeoffs: Extreme resumption speedup is largely an OpenSSL-3.x-specific lock-contention pathology, not purely an AWS-LC design win over OpenSSL 1.1.1 (gap there is much smaller, ~1.3x-1.5x); requires a non-default C11 build flag to hit peak numbers.
caveats: Independent third-party benchmark by HAProxy Technologies (Willy Tarreau, William Lallemand), published 2025-05-06, using their own open-source h1load load generator (https://github.com/wtarreau/h1load); this is a Tier-A benchmark for AWS-LC, which is already on the known-projects list, so is_evidence_for_known is set true per the harness exception rule.
found_via: Hacker News comment: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46628936 (search 'TLS faster OpenSSL', tags=comment) linking to haproxy.com/blog/state-of-ssl-stacks

name: Tempesta TLS (in-kernel TLS handshakes)
workload: Server-side full and abbreviated TLS 1.2 handshakes (ECDHE+ECDSA over NIST P-256), measured with the tls-perf tool, and full HTTPS transactions measured with wrk, comparing in-kernel Tempesta TLS handshakes against Nginx 1.19.1 + OpenSSL 1.1.1d on a 1-vCPU KVM VM (host: Intel Core i7-6500U) and on 2 bare-metal Intel Xeon E3-1240v5 servers
claimed_speedup: 40-80% more TLS connections/sec than Nginx/OpenSSL and up to 4x lower average/95th-percentile latency in the VM and bare-metal session-resumption cases; but only +6% handshake throughput for new sessions on bare metal, where Nginx/OpenSSL actually has 50-170% lower average/95th-percentile latency and Tempesta's worst-case tail latency is up to ~30x higher
hardware: 1-vCPU KVM VM on host Intel Core i7-6500U (no vAPIC); 2x bare-metal Intel Xeon E3-1240v5 with Mellanox ConnectX-2 10Gbps NICs
is_fork_of: https://github.com/ARMmbed/mbedtls (originally forked from mbed TLS 2.8.0; the paper states only PKI code remains from the original mbed TLS source, with a full rework of handshake, crypto and memory handling)
tradeoffs: Linux-kernel-module implementation (not a portable userspace library), requires modern x86-64 CPU features (AVX/BMI/ADX) with no generic C fallback, and is tightly coupled to the Tempesta FW reverse-proxy project; only covers TLS 1.2/1.3 server handshakes over P-256/x25519.
caveats: This repo (tempesta-tech/tempesta) is already in the run's KNOWN_LIST; reported only under the stated exception because this session located a peer-reviewed workshop paper (Netdev 0x14, 2020) with a fuller benchmark than what was previously catalogued. The win is non-uniform: the large 40-80%/4x figures are for the VM and session-resumption scenarios, while bare-metal new-session throughput improves only 6% alongside much worse tail latency. Compiler flags used to build Nginx/OpenSSL/Tempesta are not stated in the paper.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: HN Algolia search 'faster than openssl' surfaced the story linking to https://netdevconf.info/0x14/pub/papers/35/0x14-paper35-talk-paper.pdf ('Performance study of kernel TLS handshakes', Krizhanovsky & Koveshnikov, Netdev 0x14)
